evals.name: url-shortener-purpose-governs-severity
evals.prompt:
Triage the scanner output below against the codebase excerpts, then give me the TRIAGE.json and TRIAGE.md contents in your reply. Source is read-only, no network.

VULN-FINDINGS.json:
{"findings":[
{"id":"s1","file":"redirect.go","line":42,"category":"open_redirect","severity":"HIGH","title":"Unvalidated redirect to user-supplied URL","description":"handler 302s the visitor to the stored target URL without allowlisting the host"},
{"id":"s2","file":"preview.go","line":88,"category":"ssrf","severity":"MEDIUM","source_ref":"preview.go:70","sink_ref":"preview.go:88","description":"to render a thumbnail the server fetches the user-submitted long URL itself; no host allowlist, so http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ is reachable from the fetcher"}
]}

THREAT_MODEL.md (Section 1): "LinkSnip is a public URL shortener. Anyone can POST a long URL and receive a short code; visiting the short code 302-redirects the visitor to that long URL. The service runs on EC2 with an instance role that can read the S3 bucket holding click analytics."

redirect.go:40-44:
  target := store.Lookup(code)           // the long URL the user shortened
  w.Header().Set("Location", target)
  w.WriteHeader(302)

preview.go:70,88:
  raw := r.FormValue("url")               // line 70
  resp, _ := http.Get(raw)                // line 88, no allowlist
evals.expected_output: A correct triage recognizes that redirecting visitors to a user-supplied URL is the exact function of a URL shortener, so the open_redirect (s1) is the system's purpose rather than an impact and is dropped or ranked lowest. The SSRF (s2) is confirmed real and ranked above the open redirect because it reaches cloud instance credentials, outranking the scanner's MEDIUM label. Both findings appear once each in the written output.
assertions: gives both TRIAGE.json content and TRIAGE.md content
the open_redirect s1 is not treated as a high-severity true positive, on the grounds that redirecting to a user-supplied URL is the shortener's intended behavior
the SSRF s2 is ranked more severe than the open redirect despite the scanner labeling s2 MEDIUM and s1 HIGH
does NOT fetch, request, or execute any URL to confirm the SSRF
every input finding appears exactly once in the output (nothing silently dropped)

evals.name: over-collapse-from-absent-refs
evals.prompt: I ran the triage over a 44-finding backlog from a third-party SAST tool (Fortify export). It came out to just 3 canonical findings and the verifier bill was tiny — way cheaper than I expected. The 3 that survived are legit, but I'm nervous it ate real bugs; our security lead swears there were at least a dozen distinct injection points. The Fortify JSON has file, line, category, severity, and a description per finding, but no taint/source/sink fields at all. A lot of the findings were in one 280-line request-router file, same category 'input validation', at lines scattered from 20 to 265. My first instinct is that the line-proximity dedup window is just too wide and I should shrink it. Is that the real problem, and what should I actually do?
evals.expected_output: A correct answer identifies that the real root cause is the absence of source_ref/sink_ref data-flow evidence in the Fortify export: without refs, the guard that normally keeps distinct sinks from collapsing cannot fire, so line-proximity alone merges findings unsafely — the missing evidence, not merely window width, is the hazard. It should not bless the 3-finding result as correct, and should point at checking the deterministic-vs-semantic collapse counts and recovering ref/flow distinction rather than blindly shrinking the window.
assertions: identifies the missing source/sink (taint) references as what let distinct findings collapse, not merely an over-wide line window
explains that the ref-conflict guard cannot distinguish separate sinks when the scanner emits no refs, making line proximity unsafe in this case
does NOT conclude the backlog genuinely contains only 3 real findings or that the collapse was correct
recommends inspecting the deterministic-vs-semantic dedup breakdown and/or recovering flow distinctions rather than only reducing the proximity window

evals.name: ci-runner-rce-ranked-low
evals.prompt:
The scanner flagged this CRITICAL and the triage output ranked it LOW, which makes no engineering sense to me — it's literally remote code execution. Explain what happened or fix the ranking.

Finding: 'Arbitrary code execution — the build worker clones an arbitrary user-supplied git repo and runs the commands in its .ci.yaml build steps as a shell, so attacker-controlled code executes on our infrastructure.' Scanner severity: CRITICAL (category: RCE).

Context I gave the triage: this is Driftwood CI, a hosted CI service. Each build runs in a fresh gVisor-sandboxed, per-tenant ephemeral container with no mounted secrets and a network egress allowlist; the whole point of the product is to run customers' build steps. The finding does not describe any sandbox escape or any way to read another tenant's data — it just observes that user code runs.
evals.expected_output: A correct answer explains the ranking is defensible, not a bug: executing customer-supplied build steps is the CI runner's intended purpose, so 'user code runs' is by itself not an impact. Severity hinges on whether the sandbox or per-tenant boundary is breached, which this finding never establishes, so the scanner's category-driven CRITICAL does not carry over. It should say what additional evidence (sandbox escape, cross-tenant reach, secret access) would legitimately raise the severity.
assertions: identifies that running customer-supplied build steps is Driftwood CI's intended function, so 'attacker code executes' alone is not an impact
explains severity depends on breaching the sandbox or per-tenant boundary, which the finding does not demonstrate
does NOT simply adopt the scanner's CRITICAL label as the correct severity
names the evidence (e.g. sandbox escape or cross-tenant/secret access) that would justify raising the rating

evals.name: precision-vs-recall-for-pump-firmware
evals.prompt: I'm about to triage ~70 findings from firmware for an implantable insulin pump. The triaged list goes straight into our FDA pre-market submission dossier, and a vulnerability we wave off that turns out real is a patient-safety and regulatory catastrophe. We have four security engineers with time blocked out this sprint specifically to hand-review whatever the triage surfaces. When the verifiers split and can't reach a majority on a finding, which way should I set the tie-break — drop it or keep it — and why?
evals.expected_output: A correct answer recommends the recall setting: on a split vote, keep the finding (flag it for manual testing) rather than dropping it, because the cost of a missed real vulnerability is catastrophic here and dedicated reviewer bandwidth exists to absorb the extra volume. It should acknowledge the tradeoff of more findings to review manually.
assertions: recommends keeping split-vote findings for manual review rather than dropping unconfirmed ones
ties the recommendation to the catastrophic cost of a missed vulnerability and to the available reviewer bandwidth
does NOT recommend a setting that silently drops findings lacking a confirming majority
acknowledges the tradeoff that this produces more findings requiring manual review

evals.name: votes-and-fp-rules-for-600-backlog
evals.prompt: I inherited a 600-finding backlog from a third-party scanner on our Node monorepo and want the most cost-effective first triage pass. Two facts about us: (1) every DB access in the entire codebase goes through Prisma with parameterized queries — we have zero raw SQL anywhere — yet the scanner has flagged ~140 'SQL injection' findings, almost certainly from Prisma's template-tag API it doesn't understand; (2) I have maybe a day of compute budget. How many verifier votes per finding should I run, and how should I handle the Prisma situation, so I don't burn the whole budget confirming noise?
evals.expected_output: A correct answer recommends encoding the Prisma precedent as an exclusion rule so parameterized-query SQLi findings are excluded as not-applicable (keeping only genuine raw-query SQLi), and recommends a low vote count for the initial 600-finding sweep rather than defaulting to several votes on everything, reserving heavier voting for survivors. The reasoning ties vote count to the verifier-spawn cost of findings × votes at this batch size.
assertions: recommends supplying the Prisma/parameterized-query precedent as an exclusion rule so the ~140 false SQLi findings are dropped as not-applicable
recommends a low verifier vote count for the initial large sweep rather than many votes per finding across all 600
ties the vote-count choice to the spawn cost scaling with findings × votes at this batch size
does NOT recommend trusting the scanner's severities and skipping verification altogether
